messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lukas Weber is a 21-year-old public defender who came to treatment looking younger than his age, sharply dressed for court and visibly tense whenever there was a sudden noise in the hallway. He had come to the United States as a refugee after fleeing violence in Europe with his family in late adolescence. When he speaks about why certain moments still seize him now, the original scene comes back in fragments: a border crossing at night, a stretch of forced waiting in near-total quiet, bodies pressed low and still, everyone listening for movement, and then abrupt shouting and sharp sounds that sent people scrambling. What remains with him most clearly are not orderly memories but flashes—the outline of people crouched in the dark, the look of fear on his mother’s face, the sense of his own body folded into a cramped position and held there, afraid that any movement would draw danger.

In the months after they reached safety, Lukas did not feel that the danger had truly ended. He became convinced that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that survival depended on never letting his guard down. He was certain that you never know what can happen next, and that only constant vigilance keeps catastrophe from breaking through. That belief shaped how he managed himself: he began monitoring his own thoughts almost continuously, scanning for any sign that he might be losing control or “going crazy.” He also stopped talking with other people about what had happened or what it had done to him. In his mind, speaking about it was not relief but risk; drawing attention to it, even internally, felt unsafe. The same sense that the world was dangerous also seemed to sharpen the memories themselves. When he was already braced for harm, the past did not stay past; it returned as stark visual images and bursts of feeling that seemed to confirm he had been right all along.

Nowhere is that clearer than at work. Lukas spends his days in courtrooms, holding rooms, and noisy office corridors where metal doors slam and voices rise without warning. An ordinary bang from a file cabinet or someone calling out down the hall can make him jump hard enough to feel embarrassed in front of colleagues. At other times it is the opposite—an unusual hush outside an interview room, a pause in conversation, the silence before a hearing begins—that makes his whole body tense as if something dangerous is about to happen. In those moments he often reacts before he has consciously taken stock, with the full force of a false alarm. And when that jolt hits, the memory follows close behind: a picture-like flash, or else a wave of fear without any clear image at all, accompanied by the sensation that his body is again held in that same crouched, frozen position from the crossing.

Those intrusions have only deepened his sense that the world is perilous. When an image breaks through or his body suddenly feels as though it is back there, Lukas takes it as evidence that danger is always near and that he has to stay on guard all the time. The memories do not feel to him like recollections; they feel like proof. That same threat response then drives him further into the habits that have come to organize his life. After a startle in court or a rush of fear in a silent corridor, he immediately begins checking his mind, asking whether this is the moment he is finally breaking down. He avoids talking to coworkers or his girlfriend about what just happened, and if others bring up refugees, border stories, or the aftermath of war, he finds ways to shut the conversation down or leave.

Over time, these strategies have tightened rather than eased his fear. Because he is constantly monitoring his thoughts, every stray image or surge of feeling becomes newly significant, something to worry about and watch for. Because he avoids talking and steers away from reminders, the memories remain unprocessed and return in the same raw visual and bodily form. And because he lives this way—guarded, scanning, braced—he has come to believe even more firmly that his view of the world is simply realistic: dangerous, unpredictable, never safely quiet. His girlfriend has started telling him that he is present physically but elsewhere much of the time, especially after work, and he knows he has become harder to reach.

He finally sought help after a routine courthouse noise made him lurch in front of a client, followed by a spell of intense fear with no image attached, only the certainty that something terrible was about to happen. What frightened him most was not just the episode itself but the thought that his life was narrowing around these reactions—that he might lose his ability to do the job he cares about, or that the constant watchfulness would become permanent. At the same time, he is hoping for something simple and, to him, almost unimaginable: to sit in silence without feeling that danger is approaching, and to know that a memory is only a memory.
